summary: Herod hears of Jesus and fears John has risen; the Gospels then tell how Herod, trapped by a rash oath, had John beheaded in prison.
key_insight: When Herod heard of Jesus’ mighty works, he said, “This is John, whom I beheaded.” Herod had silenced the preacher, but he could not stop thinking about what he had done.
story: While the Twelve were out preaching, Jesus’ name became well known, and the news reached Herod, the ruler of Galilee. {Mk} People explained Jesus in different ways. Some said John the Baptist had risen from the dead, some that Elijah had appeared, and others that one of the old prophets had risen again. {Lk}

Herod was perplexed. {Lk} He told his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead, and therefore these powers are at work in him.” {Mt} And again, “This is John, whom I beheaded; he has been raised from the dead!” {Mk} Yet he also asked, “who is this of whom I hear such things?” And he wanted to see Jesus. {Lk}

The Gospels then look back. Herod had arrested John, bound him and put him in prison because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, whom he had married. John had told him, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” Herodias held it against John and wanted him dead, but she could not do it, for Herod feared John, knowing he was a just and holy man, and he protected him. When Herod heard John, he did many things, and he heard him gladly. {Mk} Herod himself wanted to put John to death, but he feared the people, because they counted John a prophet. {Mt}

Then an opportune day came. On his birthday Herod gave a feast for his nobles, the high officers and the chief men of Galilee. Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, and she pleased Herod and his guests. The king swore to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom.” {Mk}

She went out and asked her mother, “What shall I ask?” Herodias answered, “The head of John the Baptist!” The girl hurried back to the king: “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” {Mk}

The king was exceedingly sorry. Yet because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her. {Mk} He sent an executioner, and John was beheaded in prison. His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she gave it to her mother.
When John’s disciples heard of it, they came and took away his body and laid it in a tomb. Then they went and told Jesus. {Mt}
differences: Mark calls him “King Herod”; Matthew and Luke call him “Herod the tetrarch,” though Matthew also calls him “the king” later in the story.
Mark says Herodias wanted John dead while Herod feared and protected him; Matthew says Herod himself wanted to kill John but feared the people.

Only Mark names the guests (nobles, high officers and the chief men of Galilee) and records the girl’s question to her mother and the oath of “up to half my kingdom.” Matthew mentions only “those who sat with him.”
Luke records only Herod’s perplexity and his wish to see Jesus. He had already told of John’s arrest (Luke 3:19–20) and does not narrate his death.
Matthew alone says John’s disciples went and told Jesus.

fit.question: Matthew says Herod wanted to put John to death but feared the people. Mark says it was Herodias who wanted John dead, while Herod feared John and protected him. Which was it?

points.label: A divided man
points.text: Mark shows Herod pulled two ways: he feared John as a holy man and heard him gladly, yet he kept him in chains. A ruler like that could want a troublesome prophet dead in one season and protect him in another.

points.label: Two fears, one result
points.text: Matthew names the public fear, the crowds who honored John; Mark names the private one, John himself. Both fears kept John alive until the feast, and both writers say the king was sorry when the moment came.

fit.note: The two accounts show one man from two sides, and together they give a fuller picture than either alone.
fit.short: Herod was divided: at times he wanted John dead, yet he feared both the crowds (Matthew) and John himself (Mark).

scene.label: Herod Antipas
scene.text: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. Rome let him rule Galilee and Perea as tetrarch, not king, from 4 BC to AD 39. Jesus later called him “that fox” (Luke 13:32), and Antipas would question Jesus on the day of His death (Luke 23:8–9).

scene.label: Herodias
scene.text: Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great. She had been married to Antipas’s half-brother, whom the Gospels call Philip (probably not Philip the tetrarch of Luke 3:1). Antipas divorced his first wife, a Nabatean princess, to marry her. The Law forbade taking a brother’s wife (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21).

scene.label: Josephus
scene.text: The Jewish historian Josephus also tells of John’s death. He says John was held and executed at Machaerus, Herod’s fortress palace east of the Dead Sea, and that many Jews saw Herod’s later defeat in war as God’s punishment for killing John. Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

scene.label: “Up to half my kingdom”
scene.text: The words echo King Ahasuerus’s promise to Esther (Esther 5:3). Antipas had no kingdom of his own to give; he ruled only what Rome allowed. The grand oath was a boast, and it trapped him.

witnesses.matthew: Tells the story briefly and ends with John’s disciples going to tell Jesus, which leads straight into Jesus’ withdrawal and the feeding of the five thousand (14:13). Later Jesus links John’s fate to His own: “the Son of Man is also about to suffer at their hands” (17:12).
witnesses.mark: Gives the longest and most vivid account, the only extended story in his Gospel in which Jesus does not appear. He sets it between the sending of the Twelve and their return, so the cost of calling people to repent hangs over their mission. Mark alone shows Herod’s divided heart: he heard John gladly but would not let go of Herodias.
witnesses.luke: Records only Herod’s perplexity and his wish to see Jesus, a wish fulfilled at the trial (23:8). Luke had told of John’s imprisonment early (3:19–20), and here he lets Herod himself report the death: “John I have beheaded.”

seeing.reveals: Herod feared that Jesus was John come back to life. Jesus is far more: the One John prepared the way for. The forerunner’s death at a ruler’s whim points ahead to the death of Jesus at the hands of rulers, but His will be followed by a real rising.
seeing.living: Herod heard John gladly and did many things, yet he would not give up Herodias, and in the end he chose his guests’ opinion over a righteous man’s life. Enjoying God’s word is not the same as obeying it. The sin we refuse to let go of will one day ask more of us than we meant to give.
seeing.ponder: Is there a word from God you have heard gladly for years but never obeyed?

preaching.big_idea: Hearing God’s word gladly is not enough; Herod shows where refusing to repent leads.
preaching.watch_for: Mark places this flashback between the Twelve being sent (6:7–13) and their return (6:30). While the disciples preach that people should repent, Herod shows both what it costs to preach repentance and what it costs to refuse it.
